chapters.title: Every Company He Built, Bought or Lost

blocks.text: Here is the first surprise. Mukesh Ambani did not found Reliance. His father, Dhirubhai Ambani, started it in 1966 as a small textile maker. So Mukesh is not a classic start-up founder. He is something rarer: a builder who kept starting brand-new industries inside a company he inherited, and kept betting the whole company on them.

This chapter walks through every big thing he built, bought or tried to buy, in order. Some became giants. Some were taken away from him in a family split. Some were very public failures: a gas field that ran dry early, a shale gas adventure in America, a takeover bid he lost, and two mega-deals that collapsed in court rooms and board rooms. __Read the failures as carefully as the wins. They are where the lessons are.__
Watch how each project feeds the next one. That is the whole game.

blocks.name: Patalganga polyester yarn plant
blocks.idea: In the late 1970s Reliance mostly made and sold polyester cloth from its Naroda textile mill, which earned 60–70% of the company's profits. The problem: Reliance bought the yarn it wove. The idea was to make the polyester filament yarn (PFY) itself at a new plant at Patalganga, near Mumbai, so Reliance controlled its own raw material and its own margin.
blocks.decision: Mukesh was studying for an MBA at Stanford when Reliance won the licence for the polyester plant. His plan was to finish Stanford in about six months, do the World Bank's one-year Young Professionals Programme, and then come home. He told his father the plan. Dhirubhai said the plan was sensible, but that he was starting work on the plant now and would not wait one and a half years. Mukesh dropped the plan and came back immediately. That choice, a degree versus a live project, set the pattern for his whole career.
blocks.howStarted: When he joined formally, his father insisted he should have a boss. He was put under Rasikbhai Meswani, a senior family member who ran the polyester business. Mukesh later said he used his chemical engineering and business-school training to organise the project, set up reporting lines and motivate people. He was about 24. The first team was roughly 200 people.
blocks.funding: Reliance was already a listed company (its 1977 share sale was oversubscribed about seven times), so the money for projects like this came largely from the public: Mukesh has said Reliance raised money from ordinary investors up to mid-1985 and again in 1989.
blocks.whatHappened: The plant worked, and it became the first step in what business people call backward integration: making your own inputs, one step further up the chain each time. From yarn, Reliance moved on to the chemicals that make the yarn, and later to the oil that makes the chemicals. Mukesh said in 2007 that many of the first 200-odd people who built Patalganga with him were still at Reliance, running different businesses.
blocks.lesson: Say yes to the real project early. Mukesh learned more building one factory at 24 than an MBA would have taught him, and he kept the people who built it with him.

blocks.text: The first 200-odd people who built Patalganga with me are still around, running different businesses.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, interview with MoneyLIFE on Rediff, 2007

blocks.text: He kept his first team for 25 years. Loyalty is a strategy.

After Patalganga, the chain kept growing backwards. A big petrochemicals complex at Hazira in Gujarat came on stream around 1991–92, making the building blocks for polyester. Each plant made the next one possible: the profits and the know-how from one funded and staffed the next. Then came the biggest step of all.

blocks.name: Jamnagar refinery
blocks.idea: A refinery turns crude oil into petrol, diesel, jet fuel and the chemicals that Reliance's plants needed. India imported much of its fuel, and state companies dominated refining. The idea was to build a giant, modern refinery on the Gujarat coast, a short tanker trip from the Persian Gulf, and become one of the cheapest refiners on earth.
blocks.decision: Consultants told Reliance the project was not viable. One key move made it work: Reliance got an exemption from a rule that forced crude imports to go through state-owned Indian Oil, which gave it better prices and steadier supply. Mukesh chose to build one huge plant from scratch, rather than a smaller one to expand slowly, so that its size would make every barrel cheaper.
blocks.howStarted: Mukesh ran the construction himself. Forbes reported that for three years he flew from Mumbai to Jamnagar four times a week in a small Beechcraft propeller plane, a 90-minute trip each way. In 1998 a cyclone badly damaged the site. About 85,000 workers got it running again within a few weeks. The refinery started in 1999 with a capacity of 18 million tonnes of crude a year.
blocks.funding: Forbes put the refinery's cost at $3.4 billion (other reports put the whole project at about $6 billion). Part of the money came from an unusual source: a $100 million bond sold in the US that would not be repaid for 100 years, paying 10.25% interest a year. A bond is simply a loan from investors that the company promises to pay back with interest.
blocks.whatHappened: Forbes reported it came in about 30% cheaper than a comparable BP refinery in Malaysia, and earned about $10 a barrel in 2005 against about $7 for an average Singapore refinery. A second refinery was added next to it in a Special Economic Zone in 2008. Together they can process about 1.24 million barrels a day across more than 7,500 acres, with their own 2,880 MW power plant and ports.
blocks.lesson: Scale is a weapon. If you are going to build, build big enough that nobody can match your costs. But note that it took a policy exemption to make the numbers work.

blocks.text: For example: to meet green-belt rules around the refinery, the family planted about 102,000 mango trees on the land. Forbes said that was more than Emperor Akbar's famous orchard 400 years earlier.
A 100-year loan. Read that twice.

blocks.name: Reliance Infocomm (mobile phones)
blocks.idea: In 2002 mobile calls in India were expensive and mostly for the rich. Reliance Infocomm was built to change that: a nationwide phone network on cheap CDMA handsets, plus a fibre-optic backbone for data.
blocks.decision: Reliance chose to come in with enormous scale and very low prices instead of copying the existing operators. It laid the network first and priced for volume. Infocomm was launched on 28 December 2002, which would have been Dhirubhai's 70th birthday; he had died earlier that year.
blocks.howStarted: By launch day Reliance had already spent about Rs 11,000 crore and had laid about 60,000 km of optical fibre, with total planned spending of Rs 25,000 crore. The first offer, the Dhirubhai Ambani Pioneer offer, asked Rs 3,000 upfront plus Rs 600 a month for three years, with a free handset. In 2003 came Monsoon Hungama: a phone and connection for Rs 501 upfront. About half a million people signed up.
blocks.funding: The money came from Reliance Industries' own balance sheet, earned in polyester, petrochemicals and refining.
blocks.whatHappened: Infocomm shook up Indian telecom, but Mukesh lost it. In the 2005 family settlement it went to his younger brother Anil, along with Reliance Energy and Reliance Capital. Under Anil it became Reliance Communications (RCom). After Jio's later price war, RCom stopped voice calls in 2017 and filed for bankruptcy in February 2019, with debt of about Rs 50,000 crore. Mukesh had no role in that decline.
blocks.lesson: You can build something brilliant and still lose it if ownership and control are not settled. Sort out who owns what before success makes it hard.

blocks.text: This is the largest infrastructure and services rolled out by any new entrant anywhere in the world.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani at the Reliance Infocomm launch, Dec 2002 (Rediff)

blocks.name: IPCL takeover
blocks.idea: Indian Petrochemicals Corporation Ltd (IPCL) was a big government-owned petrochemicals company and a direct rival. Buying it would remove a competitor and add plants.
blocks.decision: When the government sold its controlling stake in its privatisation drive in 2002, Reliance bid and won. Buying a rival's plants was faster than building new ones.
blocks.howStarted: Reliance took management control of IPCL after buying the government's majority stake in 2002–03.
blocks.funding: Paid from Reliance's own cash and borrowings.
blocks.whatHappened: In the 2005 split IPCL went to Mukesh along with Reliance Industries. It was later merged into Reliance Industries, around 2007–08.
blocks.lesson: When a rival comes up for sale, buying can be cheaper and faster than fighting.

blocks.name: KG-D6 gas field
blocks.idea: Reliance began exploring for oil and gas under the sea off India's east coast, in the Krishna-Godavari basin. If it found gas, it could feed India's power plants and fertiliser factories and its own refinery.
blocks.decision: In a 1999 government auction of exploration blocks, Reliance won 12 of 25 blocks, more than the state-owned ONGC's 8. Mukesh told Forbes in 2006 that oil is found in the minds of men: you have to believe it is there before you drill.
blocks.howStarted: The Dhirubhai-1 and Dhirubhai-3 fields in block KG-D6 became India's first and largest deepwater gas finds to be brought into production. Reliance first proposed spending $2.47 billion to produce 40 million standard cubic metres of gas a day (mmscmd). In 2006 it raised the plan to $8.18 billion for a peak of 80 mmscmd from 31 wells.
blocks.funding: Reliance owned 60%, BP 30% and Canada's Niko Resources 10% (BP bought its 30% for about $7.2 billion). After Niko left, Reliance held about two-thirds.
blocks.whatHappened: Output began to fall short of plans from 2010, the second year of production. Only 22 wells were drilled and 18 put into production. It fell from 35.33 mmscmd in 2011–12 to 9.77 in 2013–14, and the fields stopped producing in February 2020. Estimated reserves were cut from 10.03 to 3.10 trillion cubic feet; Reliance blamed unexpected sand and water. The government blamed too few wells, disallowed $3.02 billion of costs, and in arbitration now seeks more than $30 billion from Reliance and BP. As of late 2025, the tribunal's award was still awaited.
blocks.lesson: Never build a company's story on a single forecast. Nature does not read your investor presentation.

Actual output in 2013–14

blocks.text: Promised 80, delivered under 10. Forecasts are not facts.

blocks.name: Reliance Petroleum (second Jamnagar refinery)
blocks.idea: A second, export-focused refinery right next to the first one at Jamnagar, inside a Special Economic Zone. The plan would roughly double Jamnagar into the largest refining complex on earth.
blocks.decision: Instead of funding it all from Reliance Industries, Mukesh put the project in a separate company, Reliance Petroleum Ltd (RPL), and sold shares in it to the public. That shared the cost and risk.
blocks.howStarted: RPL listed on the stock market in 2006 at Rs 60 a share. The US engineering firm Bechtel built the refinery, which started in 2008 with a crude capacity of 580,000 barrels a day.
blocks.funding: Public shareholders through the 2006 share sale, plus Reliance Industries' own stake. Forbes reported a $6 billion budget for doubling Jamnagar.
blocks.whatHappened: RPL was merged back into Reliance Industries in 2009. But the share sales around it led to a long legal fight. SEBI, India's market regulator, alleged manipulative trading by Reliance in RPL shares in November 2007. That case is told in the near-death chapter.
blocks.lesson: Separate companies can raise money for one big project, but every share trade around them gets watched closely.

blocks.name: Reliance Retail
blocks.idea: In 2006 almost all of India's shopping happened in small family shops. Mukesh wanted to build a chain of modern stores, starting with fresh fruit and vegetables bought straight from farmers, then going into electronics, fashion and groceries.
blocks.decision: At the June 2006 AGM he committed Rs 25,000 crore and said organised retail would be the overarching theme of Reliance's growth. He chose to start with food, the thing every family buys every week, rather than luxury.
blocks.howStarted: On 3 November 2006 Reliance opened 11 Reliance Fresh stores in Hyderabad, the first in Banjara Hills. The targets were huge: $25 billion of revenue in four years, a presence in 784 cities and 6,000 rural market towns by 2010, and about one million jobs.
blocks.funding: An initial Rs 10,000 crore of equity from Reliance Industries, to grow to Rs 25,000 crore. Much later, in 2020, it sold stakes to Silver Lake, KKR, GIC, TPG, Mubadala and General Atlantic at a $58.5 billion pre-money valuation, and in 2023 to Qatar's QIA and Abu Dhabi's ADIA at a $100 billion valuation.
blocks.whatHappened: The start was rough. In August 2007 traders attacked new stores in Lucknow and the Uttar Pradesh government ordered Reliance stores closed, and Reliance cut hundreds of jobs there. The 2010 targets were missed by years. But it kept going, bought brands such as Hamleys (2019, about 68 million pounds), Netmeds, Urban Ladder, Zivame, Just Dial and Metro Cash and Carry India, and in 2025–26 had revenue of Rs 3,71,085 crore and 387 million registered customers.
blocks.lesson: Big targets are fine, but local politics and small traders are real forces. Survive the bad first years and keep compounding.

blocks.text: Organised retailing will be the overarching theme of the expansion and growth of Reliance in the near-term future.

blocks.name: Petrol pumps and Jio-bp
blocks.idea: With a giant refinery, Reliance had fuel to sell. Its own branded petrol pumps would let it sell straight to drivers.
blocks.decision: By 2006 Reliance had about 1,200 pumps and Mukesh planned to grow to 6,000 for $1.5 billion. Later, he chose to bring in a partner rather than run the business alone.
blocks.howStarted: The pumps ran alongside a highway truck-stop chain, A1 Plaza, that had about 100 restaurants by 2006.
blocks.funding: Reliance's own money at first. In 2020 BP bought into the fuel retail business as part of the cash Reliance raised to cut its debt. Reliance owns 51% and BP 49% of the venture, now called Jio-bp.
blocks.whatHappened: Jio-bp operates over 1,700 fuel stations, far below the 6,000 that Mukesh planned in 2006.
blocks.lesson: When a business needs a skill you lack, a partner with that skill can be worth half the company.

blocks.name: Mumbai Indians (cricket team)
blocks.idea: In 2008 the Indian Premier League (IPL) auctioned city cricket teams. Owning one put a brand in front of hundreds of millions of fans.
blocks.decision: Reliance bid for the Mumbai franchise, its home city.
blocks.howStarted: Reliance won the team in the January 2008 auction.
blocks.funding: The winning bid was $111.9 million, paid by Reliance.
blocks.whatHappened: The team gave Reliance a permanent place in Indian cricket. Years later, IPL streaming rights also sat inside Reliance's media business.
blocks.lesson: Brands are built where attention already lives. Cricket is where India's attention lives.

blocks.name: LyondellBasell takeover bid
blocks.idea: LyondellBasell, a huge US–Dutch chemicals and refining company, was in US bankruptcy. Buying it would have made Reliance a global petrochemicals giant overnight.
blocks.decision: Mukesh decided to bid while the company was weak. In November 2009 Reliance made an unsolicited, non-binding offer of about $12 billion for control.
blocks.howStarted: Reliance's team reportedly visited the company around 20 times and revised its offer twice.
blocks.funding: The offer was planned with Reliance's cash and borrowing.
blocks.whatHappened: Reliance raised its offer to about $13.5 billion in January 2010 and about $14.5 billion in February. LyondellBasell's board said no and went with its own rescue plan, which valued it at $15.5 billion. Its largest owner, Len Blavatnik's Access Industries, called Reliance's offer too low. In March 2010 Reliance said it would not raise the bid again, saying market conditions did not justify it.
blocks.lesson: Know your walk-away price before you start. Walking away from a deal can be the winning move.

blocks.name: US shale gas
blocks.idea: Around 2010 a new drilling method opened up huge gas fields in shale rock in the US. Reliance wanted to learn the technology and own a piece of the boom.
blocks.decision: Instead of buying whole companies, Reliance bought minority stakes in joint ventures with experienced American operators: Chevron, Pioneer Natural Resources and Carrizo.
blocks.howStarted: In 2010 it paid $392 million for a 60% stake in a Marcellus shale venture in Pennsylvania, and $46 million for 49.9% of a pipeline venture in Texas's Eagle Ford region, later putting in another $208 million.
blocks.whatHappened: When oil and gas prices crashed after 2014, shale lost its shine. Reliance sold the Eagle Ford pipeline venture for $1 billion in 2015, a good result. But it sold the Marcellus assets bought for $392 million for $126 million in 2017, then other Marcellus assets for $250 million in 2021, and finally exited Eagle Ford in November 2021.
blocks.lesson: Buying into a hot trend at its peak is risky. The one profit came from the boring pipeline, not the exciting drilling.

blocks.text: Bought for $392 million. Sold for $126 million. Ouch.

blocks.name: Reliance Jio
blocks.idea: In 2010 Indians used their phones mostly for calls; data was slow and costly. Mukesh's idea was a 4G network built only for data, with voice calls carried as data and given away free, so that hundreds of millions of people could get online cheaply.
blocks.decision: After the 2005 split a non-compete deal kept him out of telecom. Within a month of the brothers ending that pact in 2010, he moved. He chose to buy a little-known company that had just won spectrum (the radio waves a phone network needs) rather than bid in his own name.
blocks.howStarted: In June 2010 Infotel Broadband, a small firm promoted by the son of HFCL's founder, became the only bidder to win broadband spectrum in all 22 telecom circles, for Rs 12,848 crore. About an hour after the auction closed, Reliance said it would buy 95% of Infotel for Rs 4,800 crore. It was later renamed Reliance Jio Infocomm. Commercial service started in September 2016.
blocks.funding: Reliance Industries funded the network from refinery profits and heavy borrowing, a bet The Economist put at about $25 billion by 2017. In 2020 it sold about a third of Jio Platforms to Facebook, Google and others for about Rs 1.52 lakh crore.
blocks.whatHappened: Jio offered free voice and very cheap data. It reached 100 million users in 170 days and passed 200 million in under two years. Rivals were forced to merge or exit. By 2025–26 it had more than 524 million subscribers, and in October 2026 Jio Platforms listed on the stock market in India's largest IPO.
blocks.lesson: If you can make something ten times cheaper, you do not compete in the market. You create a new one. But it needs patient money.

blocks.text: Jio has added seven customers every single second of every single day.

blocks.name: Network18 and media
blocks.idea: A data network needs things to watch. Owning TV channels and news sites would give Jio content and Reliance a voice in media.
blocks.decision: In 2012 Network18, a debt-laden media group run by Raghav Bahl, needed money. Reliance chose to fund it indirectly instead of buying it outright at first.
blocks.howStarted: Reliance set up a trust, the Independent Media Trust, which channelled money into Network18 and TV18 in 2012, with Network18 receiving a net Rs 4,000 crore. As part of the deal Network18 bought stakes in the ETV regional channels.
blocks.funding: Reliance Industries' cash through the trust.
blocks.whatHappened: In July 2014 Reliance took formal control of Network18 and TV18, and the founder left. A plan to merge its Viacom18 venture with Sony's India channels was dropped in 2020. Viacom18 later became the base for the much bigger Disney deal in 2024.
blocks.lesson: Control often comes in two steps: first you lend, then you own.

blocks.name: Saudi Aramco deal for the oil business
blocks.idea: Sell 20% of Reliance's oil-to-chemicals (O2C) business, the refineries and petrochemical plants, to Saudi Aramco, the world's biggest oil company. Reliance would get cash to cut debt, and a guaranteed partner for crude.
blocks.decision: Mukesh announced the plan in August 2019, valuing the business at $75 billion including debt. Aramco would also supply 500,000 barrels a day of crude to Jamnagar. It was one of the largest foreign investments ever planned for India.
blocks.howStarted: The two sides signed only a non-binding letter of intent, subject to checks and a final agreement.
blocks.funding: Aramco was to pay roughly $15 billion for the 20%.
blocks.whatHappened: Reliance first hoped to close by March 2020. It missed that date, and in July 2020 Mukesh blamed the energy market and Covid-19. In November 2021 the two companies said they would re-evaluate the deal, and Reliance withdrew its application to split off the O2C business. Reliance said its new green-energy plans had changed the picture.
blocks.lesson: A headline deal is not a deal until the money moves. Do not count it in your plan before it closes.

blocks.text: Our equity requirements have already been met.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani on the delayed Aramco deal, July 2020 (Argus Media)

blocks.text: He had already raised the money elsewhere. Always have a plan B.

blocks.name: Future Group deal
blocks.idea: Future Group, owner of Big Bazaar, was a large Indian retailer and deep in debt (over $4 billion by 2022). Buying its stores, warehouses and logistics would make Reliance Retail far bigger, fast.
blocks.decision: In August 2020 Reliance agreed to buy Future's retail, wholesale, logistics and warehousing businesses for Rs 24,713 crore (about $3.4 billion).
blocks.howStarted: There was a problem. In 2019 Amazon had bought 49% of an unlisted Future company, with a right to buy into Future Retail later. Amazon said the Reliance deal broke that contract.
blocks.funding: The price was to come from Reliance Retail, which was raising billions from global investors at the same time.
blocks.whatHappened: A Singapore arbitration panel told Future to put the deal on hold in October 2020. India's Supreme Court ruled for Amazon in August 2021. In early 2022 Reliance took over many Future stores directly from landlords when Future could not pay rent. In April 2022 Future's secured lenders voted against the deal, and Reliance called it off on 23 April 2022.
blocks.lesson: Check every contract the seller has signed. One clause in someone else's deal can freeze yours for years.

blocks.name: New Energy giga-factories
blocks.idea: Reliance earns most of its oldest money from oil. Mukesh's plan is to build the factories for the next energy system: solar panels, batteries, electrolysers that make green hydrogen, and fuel cells.
blocks.decision: At the June 2021 AGM he committed Rs 75,000 crore: Rs 60,000 crore over three years for four giga-factories, and Rs 15,000 crore for partnerships and new technology. He chose to buy technology instead of inventing all of it.
blocks.howStarted: Work began on the Dhirubhai Ambani Green Energy Giga Complex on 5,000 acres at Jamnagar. Reliance bought Norway's REC Solar for an enterprise value of $771 million and Britain's sodium-ion battery firm Faradion for about 100 million pounds, both in 2021.
blocks.funding: Reliance's own cash flow from its oil, telecom and retail businesses.
blocks.whatHappened: By the August 2025 AGM his son Anant described the Jamnagar site as the world's largest new-energy complex, still being built. Forbes reports Reliance plans to spend about $80 billion on renewables over roughly a decade.
blocks.lesson: Use today's cash cow to build tomorrow's business before you are forced to.

blocks.name: Campa Cola and consumer brands
blocks.idea: Campa Cola was an old Indian soft-drink brand. Reviving a nostalgic brand gave Reliance a fast way into packaged drinks and food.
blocks.decision: Buy an old brand with memories attached, instead of building a new one from zero.
blocks.howStarted: Reliance bought Campa in 2022 for about Rs 22 crore and relaunched it in March 2023 in three flavours, through its consumer products arm.
blocks.whatHappened: Campa now sits in Reliance Consumer Products, a unit of Reliance Retail Ventures, selling through Reliance's own stores and others.
blocks.lesson: Nostalgia is an asset you can buy cheaply. Rs 22 crore is pocket change for a household name.

blocks.name: Jio Financial Services
blocks.idea: Reliance's huge customer base could be offered loans, payments, insurance and investment products.
blocks.decision: Instead of keeping it inside Reliance Industries, Mukesh spun the finance arm off as a separate listed company. Every Reliance shareholder got one share of the new company for each Reliance share.
blocks.howStarted: It was demerged in July 2023 with about Rs 20,700 crore of cash and liquid assets, and formed a partnership with the US fund giant BlackRock for asset management.
blocks.funding: Cash and investments transferred from Reliance Industries.
blocks.whatHappened: It listed on 21 August 2023 at a price of Rs 262 set in a special trading session, then hit its daily lower limit, valuing it at about $19 billion.
blocks.lesson: Spinning off a business lets investors value it on its own, but a weak first day can follow.

blocks.name: JioStar (merger with Disney's Star India)
blocks.idea: Combine Reliance's Viacom18 and JioCinema with Disney's Star India and Hotstar to create India's largest entertainment company.
blocks.decision: First announced in February 2024. Reliance chose a merger in which it held control, instead of fighting Disney for cricket and film rights.
blocks.howStarted: After India's competition regulator approved it in August 2024, the merger took effect on 14 November 2024, with about 120 TV channels and two streaming services.
blocks.funding: Reliance put in Rs 11,500 crore. The joint venture was valued at Rs 70,352 crore (about $8.5 billion).
blocks.whatHappened: Viacom18 holds 46.82%, Disney 36.84% and Reliance directly about 16.34%, so Reliance controls about 63%. Nita Ambani is the chairperson.
blocks.lesson: Sometimes your strongest rival becomes your partner. Ask who controls the board.

blocks.text: Put the list together and a pattern jumps out. __Almost every win came from building something huge where Reliance controlled the whole chain: the yarn, the refinery, the network, the stores.__ Almost every loss came from things Mukesh could not control: geology under the sea, gas prices in America, a rival's contract, or a family split.
Control the chain, and you control the outcome. Mostly.

chapters.title: Build It Bigger Than Anyone Believes

blocks.text: Picture Mukesh in 1981. He is about 24, a chemical engineer who has just walked away from Stanford. His father would not wait a year and a half for him to finish, so he came home. Now he is on a construction site at Patalganga, working under a senior relative, with a team of about 200 people and one job: get a polyester yarn plant built.

Reliance at the time was a fast-growing but still mid-sized company. Its money machine was a single textile mill at Naroda that made 60–70% of profits. The plan Dhirubhai and Mukesh followed was simple to say and very hard to do: stop buying from suppliers, and become the supplier. First yarn. Then the chemicals that make yarn. Then the oil that makes the chemicals.
Write this down: become your own supplier, one step at a time.
Where the money came from

A start-up today raises money from venture capital funds. Reliance did something different. It raised money from ordinary Indians. When a company first sells its shares to the public, that is called an IPO, or initial public offering. Reliance did this in 1977, and the issue was oversubscribed about seven times, meaning people asked for seven times more shares than were on offer.

Mukesh has said Reliance kept raising money from the public until mid-1985, and again in 1989. Each new plant was paid for by a mix of shareholder money, borrowing and the profits from the plant before. __The trick was that every project made the next one cheaper to fund, because it proved Reliance could finish what it started.__

For example: to help fund Jamnagar, Reliance sold a $100 million bond in the US that will only be repaid after 100 years, paying 10.25% a year. Investors were lending to a company they believed would still exist in the 2090s.
The refinery nobody thought could be built

By the mid-1990s the next step was oil. Consultants said a giant private refinery in India was not viable. India also had a rule that crude imports had to go through state-owned Indian Oil. Reliance won an exemption, which gave it better prices and steadier supply. Without that one policy change, the numbers would not have worked.

Mukesh ran the build like a man possessed. For three years he flew from Mumbai to Jamnagar four times a week. In 1998 a cyclone smashed the site. About 85,000 workers got it running again within weeks. The refinery opened in 1999, and Forbes reported it was built about 30% cheaper than a comparable BP plant in Malaysia.

blocks.text: That margin is the real secret of Reliance. A refinery's margin is how much it earns on each barrel after paying for the crude. A big, complex refinery can turn cheap, heavy crude into expensive products. Jamnagar became a cash machine, and that cash paid for almost everything that came after: gas exploration, telecom, retail and, much later, Jio.
Every new business was paid for by the old one.
2002: a death, a launch and a crack

Dhirubhai Ambani died in 2002. That December, on what would have been his 70th birthday, Mukesh launched Reliance Infocomm. Reliance had already spent about Rs 11,000 crore and laid 60,000 km of fibre. The next year's Rs 501 Monsoon Hungama offer pulled in about half a million customers. The same year, Reliance took control of the state-owned rival IPCL.

After Dhirubhai's death, his two sons began fighting over who controlled what, and the row went public in late 2004. For about seven months, the feud ran in the headlines, while more than three million shareholders watched nervously.

In June 2005 their mother, Kokilaben, announced the settlement. Mukesh kept Reliance Industries, with petrochemicals, refining, oil and gas and textiles, plus IPCL. Anil got Reliance Infocomm, Reliance Energy and Reliance Capital. The group was then worth about $23 billion in revenue, equal to more than 3% of India's economy.
He lost the phone company he built. He was 48.

This was perhaps the hardest moment of his career. He had to give up Infocomm, the venture he had personally launched, and agree to stay out of his brother's businesses. __He kept the boring, giant cash machine, and that turned out to be the better half.__

blocks.text: After the split, Mukesh had a giant company and a problem: what next? He could not go back into telecom, because of the non-compete agreement with his brother. So he bet on three things at once: more refining, natural gas under the sea, and shops.

The refining bet worked. The second Jamnagar refinery, built through the separately listed Reliance Petroleum, started in 2008 and nearly doubled capacity. Together the two refineries can now handle about 1.24 million barrels a day, among the largest refining sites in the world.
Shops, and stones thrown at them

The retail bet started badly. Reliance Fresh opened 11 stores in Hyderabad in November 2006 and talked about $25 billion of sales within four years. Small traders saw it as a threat to their living. In August 2007 traders attacked new stores in Lucknow, and Uttar Pradesh chief minister Mayawati's cabinet ordered Reliance stores in Lucknow and Varanasi closed, citing the protests.

Reliance pulled back across the state. Business Today reported that 120 planned stores were scrapped and 870 staff laid off; another report put job cuts near 1,000. Protests spread to other states too. __It was a lesson that being big does not make you welcome.__ Reliance kept retail going elsewhere and quietly rebuilt over the next decade.
Big companies still need local permission. Never forget the small shopkeeper.
The gas field that ran dry

The gas bet looked like a jackpot at first. Forbes reported in 2006 that the Bay of Bengal field was first estimated at 7 trillion cubic feet and later at about twice that. In 2006 Reliance raised its development plan to $8.18 billion for 80 million cubic metres a day. BP later paid about $7.2 billion for a 30% share.

Then the numbers broke. Output began falling short from 2010. Reserve estimates were cut from 10.03 to 3.10 trillion cubic feet. By 2013–14 the field produced 9.77 million cubic metres a day, an eighth of the plan. In 2011 India's national auditor, the CAG, criticised the oil ministry for letting Reliance keep the whole block. The government disallowed billions of dollars of costs, and Reliance and BP went to arbitration.

Reliance says the problem was unexpected sand and water, not mistakes, and that government officials sat on the committee that approved every dollar. The government says Reliance drilled far fewer wells than promised. In the arbitration it now seeks more than $30 billion. Hearings ended in November 2025, and as of that date the award was still awaited.

blocks.text: An eighth of the promise. Under-promise, over-deliver. Never the reverse.
Shopping abroad, and coming home empty-handed

With cash piling up, Mukesh looked abroad. In late 2009 he went after LyondellBasell, a bankrupt chemicals giant, offering about $12 billion, then $13.5 billion, then $14.5 billion. The board said no. In March 2010 he refused to go higher. Many investors were relieved: he had shown he could walk away.

In 2010 Reliance also bought into American shale gas. It paid $392 million for 60% of a Pennsylvania venture. When gas prices collapsed after 2014, those assets lost much of their value. Reliance sold them in pieces, the first chunk in 2017 for $126 million. Only the Texas pipeline stake, sold for $1 billion in 2015, made a clear profit. By November 2021 Reliance had left US shale completely.
The regulator comes calling

A legal shadow also began in this period. SEBI, India's stock market regulator, alleged that in November 2007 Reliance had traded shares of Reliance Petroleum in a manipulative way. In a 2017 order SEBI found manipulation and imposed a trading ban on Reliance, along with an order to give up about Rs 447 crore of gains plus interest.

In January 2021 SEBI fined Reliance Rs 25 crore and Mukesh personally Rs 15 crore, with two other firms also fined. In December 2023 the Securities Appellate Tribunal set aside the penalties on Mukesh and two other firms. It noted that Reliance's board had given two other people the power to decide the share sale, and that a managing director is not automatically responsible for every breach. In November 2024 the Supreme Court dismissed SEBI's appeal against the relief given to Mukesh, while a part involving Reliance itself remained before the court.
Cleared personally, after 16 years. Legal fights are slow and costly.
The all-in bet

By 2010 the brothers had ended their non-compete pact. Within a month, Mukesh was back in telecom. On 11 June 2010 Infotel Broadband, an almost unknown company, won broadband spectrum in all 22 circles for Rs 12,848 crore. Business Today asked the obvious question: who is Infotel, and how does it have that kind of money? An hour after the auction closed, the answer came. Reliance would buy 95% of it for Rs 4,800 crore.

For six years Reliance built quietly. It renamed Infotel as Reliance Jio Infocomm in 2013, switched its own staff onto the network in December 2015, and kept pouring in money from Jamnagar and from loans. __This was the moment Mukesh bet the whole company again, just as his father had done with each new plant.__

chapters.title: Free Calls, Giant Cheques, Record IPO

blocks.text: On 1 September 2016, at Reliance's annual general meeting, Mukesh announced Jio's welcome offer: free voice calls, no roaming charges and very cheap data. Commercial service began days later. India had never seen anything like it. In the first month about 16 million people signed up.

The growth was absurd. Jio hit 50 million users in 83 days and 100 million in 170 days. By February 2017 its users were consuming more than 100 crore GB of data a month. When Jio finally started charging, its Jio Prime plan cost Rs 303 a month for unlimited data.
For example: Jio added customers at about seven every second, day and night, for its first 170 days. That is roughly the population of a small town every hour.
He was 59 when he launched Jio. It is never too late.
The price war

A price war is when companies keep cutting prices to win customers, even if it means losses. Jio's free calls forced every rival to cut. Bharti Airtel reportedly spent more on its network in two years than in the previous 20. Vodafone and Idea merged to survive. Of the 16 or so operators in the market, most were pushed out or swallowed, leaving India heading towards just a handful.

One of the casualties was close to home. Reliance Communications, the old Infocomm now run by Anil, stopped voice services in December 2017 and filed for bankruptcy in February 2019. __The brother who got the phone company lost it to the brother who was banned from phones for five years.__

blocks.text: The debt mountain

All this cost a fortune. By 31 March 2020 Reliance's net debt, meaning its loans minus its cash, had reached Rs 1,61,035 crore, about $21 billion. Mukesh had publicly promised shareholders he would make Reliance net-debt-free by 31 March 2021. Then Covid-19 hit, energy markets were thrown into turmoil, and the Aramco deal he was counting on stalled.
A public promise, then a pandemic. Pressure like this breaks people.
58 days that changed everything

What happened next is one of the great fundraising sprees in business history. In April 2020, in the middle of India's lockdown, Facebook agreed to pay Rs 43,574 crore (about $5.7 billion) for 9.99% of Jio Platforms, the holding company for Jio and Reliance's digital apps. Then came Silver Lake, Vista, General Atlantic, KKR, Mubadala, ADIA, TPG, L Catterton and Saudi Arabia's PIF, one after another, sometimes a few days apart.

In June Reliance also raised about $7 billion from its own shareholders in a rights issue, which is when a company offers existing shareholders new shares at a discount. It was India's largest ever. On 19 June 2020 Reliance announced it had raised Rs 1,68,818 crore in 58 days and was net-debt-free, nine months ahead of the promise.
I have fulfilled my promise to the shareholders by making Reliance net debt-free much before our original schedule of 31st March 2021.

In July 2020 Google joined too, paying Rs 33,737 crore for 7.7% of Jio Platforms. In total, Jio sold about a third of itself for about Rs 1.52 lakh crore. The retail arm then raised about $4.4 billion more from GIC, TPG, Mubadala, General Atlantic, Silver Lake and KKR, at a $58.5 billion valuation before the new money. __The lesson: he sold minority stakes to the world's best investors, but never control.__

blocks.text: Very important for founders: sell slices, keep the steering wheel.
Two deals that died

Not everything worked. The Future Group purchase, agreed in August 2020 for Rs 24,713 crore, got stuck in Amazon's legal challenge. In April 2022 Future's secured lenders voted it down and Reliance walked away, though it had already taken over many Future stores from landlords. The Aramco deal, announced at a $75 billion valuation for the oil business, was shelved in November 2021.
The secured creditors of FRL have voted against the scheme.

blocks.text: Media, money and a new energy bet

Mukesh kept stacking businesses. In 2021 he committed Rs 75,000 crore to green energy. In 2023 he spun off Jio Financial Services, which listed at Rs 262 a share and immediately fell to its daily lower limit. In November 2024 Reliance and Disney merged their Indian media businesses into JioStar, valued at Rs 70,352 crore, with Reliance in control.

Meanwhile the old oil business found a new and controversial edge. After Russia invaded Ukraine and Western countries capped the price of Russian oil, Reliance bought much more Russian crude. It rose from 3% of Jamnagar's crude imports in 2021 to an average of about 50% in 2025, according to the research group CREA. Reliance signed a 10-year supply deal with Rosneft, and in 2025 the US cited India's Russian oil purchases when it put an extra 25% tariff on Indian goods.
Cheap crude is a great margin. It is also geopolitics.
October 2026: the Jio IPO

Back in 2019 Mukesh had said Jio and Retail should list within five years. Jio's turn came in October 2026. Jio Platforms filed its final prospectus on 14 October, offering 27 crore new shares at Rs 1,065–1,119 each, about Rs 30,213 crore in all. No existing shareholder sold. About Rs 27,500 crore was planned to repay debt at Reliance Jio Infocomm.

Demand was enormous. The issue was fully subscribed in about 100 minutes and closed 22.19 times oversubscribed, with bids worth more than Rs 7.4 lakh crore from about 1.39 crore applications. On 28 October 2026 the shares opened at Rs 1,358, 21.36% above the issue price. It was India's largest IPO ever, beating Hyundai India's Rs 27,870 crore.

blocks.text: Here is the wow detail. On listing day Jio Platforms alone was worth about Rs 12.5 lakh crore, which made it India's second most valuable company. Only its own parent, Reliance Industries at about Rs 16.19 lakh crore, was bigger. A company that did not exist in 2010 was worth more than three-quarters of the empire that built it.
Started in 2010. Worth $131 billion in 2026.
How the fortune actually grew

Mukesh's wealth is mostly his family's controlling stake in Reliance Industries, which in 2012 was reported at about half the company. When Forbes profiled him in 2006, he was 49 and worth about $8.5 billion. On 29 October 2026, Forbes' real-time list put him at $80.5 billion, the 25th richest person in the world.

The engine underneath is simple. In 2025–26 Reliance had revenue of Rs 11,75,919 crore, profit after tax of Rs 95,754 crore and 4,19,911 employees. Oil-to-chemicals still brought the most revenue, Rs 6,62,401 crore, but the digital business earned the most operating profit (EBITDA, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation), Rs 76,560 crore, against Rs 60,546 crore for oil-to-chemicals. Retail added Rs 3,71,085 crore of revenue.

__So the fortune grew in layers: polyester paid for petrochemicals, petrochemicals for the refinery, the refinery for Jio, and Jio, now listed, is the most valuable new layer.__ Forbes reports Mukesh announced plans in 2026 to invest about $110 billion in AI infrastructure across India over seven years. The next layer is already being poured.
Our vision is global, but our purpose remains deeply Indian.

factCheck.method: Written for part-2 (business story). Primary and near-primary sources were read directly where reachable: Reliance's Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 page, Mukesh Ambani's 2007 MoneyLIFE interview on Rediff, Rediff's 2002 and 2006 launch reports, Forbes 2006 magazine profile and Forbes real-time profile (29 Oct 2026), Al Jazeera (2005 split, 2025 Russian oil), TechCrunch (2020, 2022, 2023, 2024), KrASIA (2020 debt-free), Scroll (Future deal), Argus Media and Offshore Technology (Aramco), Outlook India (KG-D6, Dec 2025), Millennium Post/PTI (shale exit), Business Today (2010 Infotel, 2018 Jio), TelecomTalk (2017), India TV News (Jio IPO listing, 28 Oct 2026), SportCal (JioStar), The Tribune/PTI and Outlook Business (SEBI/SAT/Supreme Court). Several Indian outlets (Economic Times, Mint, The Hindu, Financial Express, India Today, Business Standard) and NYT/Economist/Bloomberg/CNBC could not be fetched directly; for these, facts were taken from search-engine extracts of the cited page, and Economist/Bloomberg items rely on the headline only. Wikipedia pages are listed as leads; facts cited to them (Hazira date, IPCL, RPL listing price, Mumbai Indians bid, Campa, Hamleys and other retail acquisitions, Network18 trust, Jio-bp outlet count, JFS cash) were not independently re-read at the original source because this session's web-search budget ran out, and should be checked by the fact-checker. The 2021 Aramco shelving report (Udayavani/PTI) was found via search, but the page later returned 404; the claim matches Argus's account of delays.
